narrative: No prior evidence is available, so this first iteration registers a broad, falsifiable screen for measured predictor subgroups that are associated with stronger dependency (more negative CRISPR dependency scores). I prioritized comparisons with large, complete cell sizes: mostly binary features with exposed counts well above 20, plus one categorical feature with known sufficiently large levels. Outcomes were spread across all 16 dependency scores, with early positions emphasizing higher-variance scores that are more likely to reveal large differences. Each proposal compares the predictor-positive group, or the non-modal level_002 for feature_054, against the predictor-negative/modal level, expecting a negative exposed-minus-comparator mean difference, i.e., stronger dependency in the exposed group. Direction is set to -1 to make the evidence signed to that same stronger-dependency hypothesis. These are association hypotheses in this dataset only, not causal claims. Later I will judge whether point estimates and 95% intervals imply differences large enough relative to the 10% clinical-significance guideline, and then pursue interactions or validation only for promising main-effect signals.

Because this is iteration 1 and there is no prior evidence, I propose a broad but feasible screening set focused on measured binary predictors and one common two-level nominal predictor. Binary predictors are preferred because group sizes are transparent from the supplied counts and most have at least 100 observations in the exposed or unexposed category, reducing the risk of failing the minimum 20 observations per comparison cell. I also prioritize outcomes with larger SD or unusual means, especially outcome_001, outcome_014, outcome_006, outcome_013, outcome_011, and outcome_008, because these appear to carry more outcome variability and may be more likely to reveal dependency heterogeneity. The negative-direction hypotheses represent stronger dependency in the exposed group, i.e. a raw exposed-minus-comparator mean difference that is more negative. The positive-direction hypotheses represent weaker dependency or possible resistance-like phenotype in the exposed group. Interaction hypotheses ask whether the effect of a ~20% prevalence marker is modified by a ~50% prevalence subgroup marker. I avoid continuous and poorly balanced categorical predictors in this first round because the controller may require cell-count safety and because nominal levels with sparse cells could be underpowered. The 10% relative-dependency rule is interpreted practically by outcome scale: for standard outcomes with means around -0.25, a signed clinical effect is near 0.025 in the claimed direction; for outcome_001 it is nearer 0.04; for outcome_014 and outcome_006, whose means are near zero, relative scaling is unstable, so I would judge those using a similar absolute shift around 0.025 rather than a literal 10% of a near-zero mean. These analyses are associational in the supplied dataset only; correlated predictors, confounding, and generalizability remain unresolved.

Initial exploration prioritizes claims with adequate group sizes and scientific interpretability. I focus on balanced binary markers (feature_034, feature_002, feature_060), moderately prevalent binary markers, and the only categorical exposure with confidently sufficient minor-group counts (feature_054: level_002 vs level_001). Direction +1 represents a claim that the exposed-minus-comparator difference is positive in raw scale, corresponding to weaker dependency; direction -1 represents a claim that the raw difference is negative, corresponding to stronger dependency. Interactions and eligibility restrictions test whether continuous biomarker context changes dependency relationships. Because dependency scores are often centered around negative values and low variance, I will treat effects near 10% of the relevant absolute outcome scale as clinically meaningful, while giving extra weight to larger absolute differences on noisier outcomes such as outcome_001, outcome_008, outcome_011, outcome_013, outcome_014, and outcome_006. All comparisons are registered as unresolved because no evidence exists yet.

No claims or evidence exist yet, so the initial stage should generate falsifiable discovery comparisons rather than assess conclusions. I registered a breadth-first set of main-effect hypotheses across all outcomes, ordered so that the first 12 proposals cover distinct outcomes and likely enter analysis. Prevalent binary features (feature_008, feature_030, feature_047, feature_064, feature_023) are tested with direction +1, anticipating that the exposed=1 group may show weaker dependency (higher/less negative CRISPR dependency score), which is a plausible alternative to stronger dependency and therefore useful for broad exploration. Rarer binary features or the categorical level feature_054=level_002 are tested with direction -1, anticipating stronger dependency (more negative scores). Interaction hypotheses are registered for high-variance outcomes where heterogeneity among binary biomarker states is plausible: outcome_001 feature_034 effect modified by feature_002; outcome_006 feature_050 effect modified by feature_060; outcome_014 feature_054 effect modified by feature_045; and outcome_008 feature_045 effect modified by feature_034. For each, the anticipated interaction direction is negative, meaning the exposed-minus-comparator contrast is expected to be more negative in the biomarker-positive subgroup than in the complement. All initial statuses are unresolved because no data have been analyzed. Future assessments will require not only statistical exclusion of the null but also an effect size that is meaningful relative to the outcome scale and adequate cell counts. Any conclusions will be limited to this supplied dataset unless validated independently.

This first batch of 12 hypotheses tests main effects of three balanced binary predictors (feature_002, feature_034, feature_060) on four dependency outcomes selected for larger dispersion and sufficiently negative baseline means (outcome_001, outcome_008, outcome_011, outcome_013). The expected raw contrast is negative for exposed vs comparator because more negative dependency scores indicate stronger CRISPR dependency; I hypothesize that exposure=1 marks a biology associated with greater dependency. The clinically meaningful threshold is treated as at least about 10% relative difference versus the outcome-specific mean absolute score, e.g. outcome_001 ~0.0415, outcome_011 ~0.0301, outcome_013 ~0.0269, outcome_008 ~0.0282. Alternative hypotheses are no association or exposure associated with weaker dependency (less negative scores). These are initial discovery comparisons, not causal claims; follow-up will expand to other outcomes, categorical predictors, high-prevalence binary markers, continuous/thresholded predictors, and interactions only if signals are promising.

First-iteration plan: register a broad set of directional hypothesis tests that are likely to be well powered given the supplied dataset. The dataset contains many fully observed binary predictors with sufficient minority-group counts, so these are used for primary mean_difference comparisons. For binary exposures, exposed=1 is compared with comparator=0. For categorical exposures, labels are compared directly. A negative raw exposed-minus-comparator difference indicates that the exposed group has a more negative CRISPR dependency score, i.e., stronger dependency. Where direction=-1 and anticipated_direction=-1, the hypothesis is that exposure is associated with stronger dependency. Where direction=+1 and anticipated_direction=+1, the hypothesis is that exposure is associated with weaker dependency, i.e., a less negative score. These are falsifiable subgroup-association claims, not causal claims. The main alternatives are no association or the opposite direction. The selected outcomes include those with larger variability or less near-zero mean where a raw mean difference may be easier to detect, while still sampling across the dependency-score outcomes. Selected exposures include high-prevalence binary markers and two categorical markers whose level counts appear adequate for Welch comparisons. After these analyses, the next iterations will prioritize predictors/outcomes with evidence of clinically meaningful differences, test complementary outcomes not covered here, and use interactions or subgroup refinements only when main-effect evidence suggests biological heterogeneity. Independent validation will be considered for robust associations, with uncertainty and the 10 percent relative-difference threshold used in context; because some dependency-score means are close to zero, absolute differences and interval estimates will also guide clinical significance judgments.

At the first explore stage I registered a broad but powered set of comparisons for the 16 CRISPR dependency outcomes. I prioritized binary predictors with prevalence large enough to provide at least 20 observations in exposed and comparator cells, especially markers with approximately 20-50% exposed prevalence or balanced prevalence, because these give the best early power to detect differences. I selected several higher-variance dependency outcomes (for example outcome_014, outcome_006, outcome_001, outcome_008, outcome_013, and outcome_011) plus several lower-variance but biologically representative dependency outcomes to identify predictors with possible outcome-specific effects. For each mean_difference claim, exposure=1 denotes the presence of the measured marker and comparator=0 denotes absence. Because more negative dependency scores indicate stronger CRISPR dependency, the scientific hypothesis is that the exposed marker is associated with a more negative outcome, i.e. a raw exposed-minus-comparator mean difference below zero. Therefore I registered direction=-1 and anticipated_direction=-1, so a positive signed evidence estimate would indicate support for the hypothesis. I also registered two interaction claims to test whether a binary marker's association is stronger in a predefined high stratum: an interaction for outcome_014 using feature_034 with feature_061 threshold at 50, and an interaction for outcome_006 using feature_045 within feature_002=1 versus its complement. These are exploratory associations in the supplied dataset only, not causal claims. For later appraisal, I will consider an effect scientifically meaningful only if it is in the hypothesized direction, has a 95% interval that is sufficiently away from zero, and has an absolute mean difference large enough to plausibly exceed the 10% relative clinical-significance threshold; given typical outcome magnitudes around 0.25 absolute, I will regard differences of roughly 0.03-0.05 dependency units and especially larger as candidates for acceptance, with uncertainty guiding the final conclusion.

This is an initial broad exploration designed to identify which measured predictors show large differences in high-variance CRISPR dependency scores. Because predictor names are opaque, the comparisons are data-driven associations rather than biologically motivated causal claims. I prioritized outcomes with relatively large spread and potentially meaningful dynamic range: outcome_001, outcome_006, and outcome_014. For each outcome I tested major binary or categorical predictors with reasonably large comparison cells: feature_034, feature_002, feature_060, and feature_054. The directional hypothesis is that the exposed group has stronger dependency, i.e., a more negative dependency score than the comparator. Since more negative values mean stronger dependency, the anticipated raw exposed-minus-comparator contrast is negative. Each claim therefore uses direction = -1; a positive signed estimate would support the stated hypothesis. For feature_060, I defined exposed = 0 and comparator = 1 to test whether the zero state may mark stronger dependency, while for feature_034 and feature_002 I tested the one state. Feature_054 compares level_002 to level_001. The 10% relative-difference threshold is important: outcome_006 and outcome_014 have means close to zero, so relatively small absolute differences can be proportionally large, whereas outcome_001 requires a somewhat larger absolute difference to reach the same relative threshold. These results will guide later focused follow-up, including interactions, subgroup effect modification, and reversed-direction refinements if the observed contrast is large but opposite to the anticipated direction.

No claims are available yet, so this is an initial binary-predictor screen for association with CRISPR dependency. Dependency scores are more negative when dependency is stronger. Most proposals therefore use negative direction to test whether an exposure status is associated with stronger dependency; a few use positive direction to test whether exposure status is associated with weaker/less negative dependency. For negative-direction claims, a positive signed estimate supports stronger dependency in the exposed group relative to the comparator. For positive-direction claims, a positive signed estimate supports weaker dependency in the exposed group relative to the comparator. All selected predictors are binary or near-binary numeric features with both groups represented; common-marker hypotheses expose the minority absent value where the group size is still large enough for discovery. I avoided feature_049 because it is constant, and avoided categorical variables whose minority levels could not be verified to have at least 20 observations from the supplied summary. This first wave is deliberately broad but executable, covering 12 outcomes and testing both dependency-enhancing and dependency-reducing directions. Later results will guide follow-up around outcomes with wider dispersion (for example outcome_001, outcome_006, outcome_008, outcome_011, outcome_013, outcome_014) and predictors with sufficiently large cell counts.

Initial screen: feature_002, feature_034, and feature_060 are complete binary predictors with roughly balanced exposure/comparator counts, so Welch comparisons should have good power and satisfy the minimum-cell-count rule. They are tested against four representative outcomes: outcome_012 as a typical CRISPR dependency score; outcome_001 because it has a more negative mean dependency and larger spread; outcome_014 because it appears more heterogeneous; and outcome_006 because it also has broad dispersion. Directions are left uncertain because predictor labels are opaque and no reliable prior mechanistic direction is available. For these representative outcomes, a clinically meaningful difference is approximately a 10% relative shift in dependency score; with typical means near -0.25 to -0.42, this corresponds to absolute differences around 0.02-0.04, except outcome_014's near-zero mean will require extra caution when interpreting relative significance. These tests are association/hypothesis-generating, not causal claims.

Starting a broad first pass across CRISPR dependency scores, prioritizing binary measured features with enough sample size to meet the minimum cell-size rule and several outcome scores with clear negative means or higher dispersion. Most hypotheses are signed negative because more negative dependency scores mean stronger dependency, and a positive common biomarker could mark a lineage/state with stronger essential-gene reliance. I deliberately include both direct mean contrasts and interaction contrasts to test whether measured covariates modify the biomarker-dependency relationship: older age (feature_061), a high continuous measured score (feature_018), higher log-pfs-like measure (feature_043), and a common categorical stratum (feature_009 level_003). Rare binary markers feature_032 and feature_022 are included as main effects because their exposed groups remain above 20 observations overall, but their directions are marked uncertain. Later conclusions will require effect sizes consistent with at least about a 10% relative difference in the dependency score and uncertainty intervals compatible with scientific meaningfulness.

I register a first discovery set that prioritizes complete binary predictors and outcomes with informative scale and variance. More negative CRISPR dependency scores indicate stronger dependency, so negative-direction claims hypothesize stronger dependency in the exposed group, while positive-direction claims hypothesize weaker dependency. The main-effect set samples several outcome distributions and prevalence strata, and the interaction set tests whether a biomarker's association with dependency is context-dependent across common co-occurring states. All initial claims are unresolved pending 95 percent Welch intervals and evaluation against the 10 percent relative-difference threshold. Plausible alternatives for every registered comparison are no association or the opposite sign because the labels are opaque and the dependency outcomes may reflect distinct genetic or cellular contexts.

No prior claims exist. This first round registers a balanced discovery screen for common binary predictors and a few effect-modification hypotheses. Outcomes are selected for informative variance and distinct score distributions: outcome_014 (least negative mean), outcome_006 (broad spread), outcome_001 (more negative mean and wide spread), and outcome_013 (heavy-tailed negative dependency). Exposure feature_002, feature_034, feature_060, feature_045, and feature_021 are common binary labels with enough rows for Welch discovery. Direction convention: more negative dependency score means stronger dependency; a negative hypothesis direction means exposed-minus-comparator is expected to be more negative, and a positive direction means exposed is expected to have a less negative score. Because predictor labels are opaque, I deliberately register both biologically plausible directions: marker presence for feature_002/feature_060/feature_021 is hypothesized to increase dependency, while marker presence for feature_034/feature_045 is hypothesized to decrease dependency. Plausible alternatives include the opposite sign, a null main effect, or a subgroup-only effect. The three interaction proposals test whether the dependency contrast for feature_002 differs by feature_034 or feature_060, and whether the feature_034 contrast differs in high versus lower feature_044. These are dataset-specific associations only; causality and generalizability are not assumed.

No prior claims exist, so I am registering a first wave of discovery comparisons. Because predictor labels are opaque, I focus on comparisons with clear statistical power and plausible scientific interpretability: binary predictors with adequate prevalence and continuous feature_061 as a clinically-like numeric subgroup. Main effects test whether the exposed group has a more negative dependency score (direction -1; stronger dependency) or a more positive score (direction +1; weaker dependency). Interactions test whether the exposed-minus-comparator contrast is more negative or more positive in the named subgroup than in the subgroup complement. I choose relatively common binary features to satisfy the 20-observed-cell rule, and I include age/continuous-feature subgroups to begin testing effect modification. The reported signed effects will be judged against the 10% relative clinical-significance threshold and 95% intervals, with particular attention to whether confidence limits exclude the threshold or remain too wide to support acceptance. These are associations only, not causal claims.

This corrected registration avoids the earlier eligibility/subgroup overlap by using a distinct common binary eligibility for continuous-subgroup interactions. I focus on binary predictors with adequate exposed/comparator cell sizes and on dependency outcomes with higher dispersion, where associations are more likely to be estimable. For negative-direction claims, exposed=1 is hypothesized to have a more negative dependency score than comparator=0, meaning stronger CRISPR dependency; positive-direction claims hypothesize weaker dependency. The direct mean_difference hypotheses test whether feature_002, feature_034, feature_060, feature_045, feature_052, feature_065, and feature_050 identify subgroups with altered dependency across different outcome models. The interaction hypotheses test whether the feature_034 or feature_002 contrast differs in high feature_061 versus lower feature_061, and in high feature_043 versus lower feature_043, among participants with feature_008=1. These are falsifiable associations in the supplied dataset only, not causal statements or claims of generalizability. If estimates and 95% Welch intervals favor the signed direction and approach/exceed the 10% relative-difference benchmark, follow-up will stratify the effect and extend the predictor to additional outcomes.

This is the first exploration pass, so I register a broad but pre-specified set of 12 binary biomarker/covariate contrasts across 12 CRISPR dependency outcomes. Because predictor names are opaque, I avoid assuming clinical meaning and instead treat measured binary status or a known two-level categorical predictor as the exposure. This supports scientifically falsifiable statements while remaining conservative about interpretation. Dependency scores are oriented such that more negative values mean stronger dependency. Therefore, a raw exposed-minus-comparator mean difference <0 corresponds to stronger dependency in the exposed group; I encode that as claim direction -1. Two contrasting hypotheses encode the alternative biology where a measured marker might indicate redundancy, resistance, or reduced pathway dependence, yielding a less negative score; these use direction +1. I selected complete binary predictors with prevalences far from 0 or 1 so that both comparison cells exceed 20 observations. I included higher-variance and distinctive outcomes such as outcome_001, outcome_006, and outcome_014 to increase sensitivity to meaningful shifts, while also surveying several more conventional dependency outcomes. For these negative-mean outcomes, the 10% clinical-significance threshold is roughly 0.009-0.042 score units depending on the outcome mean, so intervals and effect magnitude will be judged against that practical scale. All claims are initially unresolved.

This is the first discovery pass with no registered evidence, so I registered main-effect comparisons only and deliberately chose predictors whose marginal group counts are sufficient for stable Welch comparisons. Rare levels with uncertain per-level counts and continuous predictors without a defined threshold were deferred to reduce invalid cells. Binary numeric exposures use 1 vs 0; feature_054 uses its two observed nominal levels. The direction convention is: direction -1 tests whether the exposed group has a more negative CRISPR dependency score, i.e., stronger dependency; direction +1 tests whether the exposed group has a less negative/higher score, i.e., weaker dependency. Most rare or balanced markers are registered as vulnerability candidates (more negative dependency), whereas high-prevalence markers such as feature_008 and feature_047 are registered with the opposite direction as a scientific alternative: common marker status may be associated with less vulnerability. Outcomes were spread across the 16 dependency scores, with emphasis on outcome_001, outcome_006, outcome_013, and outcome_014 because these have larger dispersion and may reveal clinically meaningful relative differences more readily. All initial statuses are unresolved because no effect has been observed yet. Future follow-up should prioritize predictors with effects approaching or exceeding the 10% relative-difference threshold, then test the same predictors across correlated outcomes and, when subgroup cells are large enough, test interactions. These are association hypotheses only and do not imply causality or generalizability beyond this dataset.

No prior claims exist, so the first screen focuses on predictors with adequate cell sizes and dependency outcomes that are either highly variable or clinically interesting as negative-score outcomes. Binary predictors such as feature_034, feature_002, feature_060, feature_021, and feature_027 provide balanced exposure groups, while feature_001 tests a rarer marker with still adequate exposed count. The negative-direction hypotheses state that the exposed group has a more negative dependency score, i.e. stronger CRISPR dependency; positive-direction hypotheses state that the exposed group has a higher, less negative score, implying weaker dependency. Interaction hypotheses test whether a second marker modifies the exposure-outcome relationship in the same eligible population. All hypotheses are initially unresolved because magnitude and uncertainty must be evaluated against Welch intervals and the 10% relative difference criterion, with additional attention to absolute dependency-score differences because some outcome means are close to zero.

No prior ledger evidence exists, so iteration 1 registers a broad but tractable set of main-effect hypotheses spanning the outcome set. I prioritize outcomes with comparatively larger dispersion and/or more distinctive dependency distributions (outcome_014, outcome_006, outcome_001, outcome_011, outcome_008, outcome_013) while still covering additional CRISPR dependency scores. Exposures are restricted to measured binary or two-level categorical features with large enough cells for the 20-observation cell-count rule. Because predictor labels are opaque, the directional assignments are exploratory hypotheses about whether an exposure level behaves like a dependency-enhancing or dependency-reducing marker, not causal biological claims. For outcome_014 and outcome_006, which have less-negative mean scores, I register positive-direction hypotheses (exposure associated with weaker dependency, i.e., higher score). For most remaining rare or binary marker exposures, I register negative-direction hypotheses (exposure associated with stronger dependency, i.e., more negative score), and for the categorical feature_054 comparison I test whether level_002 has stronger dependency than level_001. All comparisons start unresolved. Later, large estimates, interval widths, and whether the effect size plausibly crosses the 10% relative-difference threshold will guide refinement, reversal, subgroup interaction testing, and optional validation.

This is an initial broad screening round. Because the predictor labels are opaque, I prioritize complete binary predictors with adequate group sizes to avoid Welch-cell-count failures, and I include balanced binary variables as subgroup strata so interaction contrasts can be estimated with sufficient cells in both the subgroup and complement. I also include outcomes with higher dispersion or more negative mean dependency scores, where clinically meaningful relative shifts may be detectable. For most CRISPR outcomes with mean near -0.25, a 10% relative difference corresponds roughly to an absolute mean difference of about 0.02-0.03; for outcome_001 (mean about -0.42) the threshold is about 0.04, while outcome_014 and outcome_006 have lower absolute means and therefore lower absolute thresholds. Directional hypotheses are pre-specified: exposure markers are hypothesized to indicate either pathway activation/relevance (stronger dependency, direction -1 for a more negative score) or possible redundancy/resistance (weaker dependency, direction +1 for a higher score). These comparisons are intended only as discovery in the supplied dataset and do not imply causality or generalizability.
